title: Five Ways: Tackling Common Learning Barriers
author: Tom Sherrington
summary: Tom Sherrington, arguing that teachers face too many competing ideas from cognitive science to track simultaneously, distills five headline barriers to learning worth keeping constantly in mind. Attention deficits require systematic checks (cold calling, show-me boards, structured pair-share) rather than assuming attention is present. Lack of prior knowledge means teachers must evaluate their own assumptions about what vocabulary, references, or experiences students actually have before building on them. Cognitive overload and transience -- a concept he credits to Oliver Caviglioli -- describes information disappearing (verbally or via slide changes) before students have had time to process it, addressed by keeping examples visible, writing down key points, and using dual-coded visual supports. Poor fluency of recall results from moving between concepts without enough consolidation, leaving students with sketchy, poorly connected schemas. Task completion as a false proxy for learning warns that students can fill notebooks with copied diagrams and borrowed answers while doing almost no independent thinking, meaning teachers cannot assume completed work equals learning unless the task genuinely required independent thought.
points: Sherrington explicitly rejects the common pushback that a 'barriers to learning' list should include social-emotional issues, arguing the most useful thing a teacher can do in the moment is help students feel successful as learners regardless of what else is happening.

His cognitive-overload-and-transience barrier (credited to Oliver Caviglioli) reframes a familiar CLT concern into a concrete fix: keep information visible rather than letting slides or verbal explanations disappear before students have processed them.

The task-completion barrier directly challenges a default teacher heuristic -- 'the work is in the books, so learning happened' -- by cataloguing how much can be copied, borrowed, or trivially matched without real thinking.

Sherrington's closing recommendation for the task-completion barrier is counterintuitive: sometimes it's better to hand students a ready-made table or diagram and spend saved time on checks for understanding, rather than have them copy it themselves under the illusion that copying is learning.
quotes: There are SO MANY issues that teachers have to think about every lesson just to run the room and work through the curriculum.
The key thing is not to just expect or hope for attention – it's to require it through the structure of your means of participation: cold calling, show-me boards, pair-share.
Ever since Oliver Caviglioli shared his view that cognitive load theory largely comes down to the problem of transience, I’ve noticed it in lessons over and over again.

It's actually remarkable how much students can do in this way without learning much: copy diagrams; write out worked examples; copy model paragraphs; create tables of information, 'borrow' answers from their neighbours.
You can't assume that the look of the work on the page represents learning outcomes unless the task absolutely required independent thinking.
It’s always more helpful in the long run to build secure foundations than to rush through content in a half-learned, surface manner.
